---
title: "Gold & Treasury Yields — Introduction"
author: "Gregoire MANSIO"
format: html
---

## Motivation

Gold is one of the most studied assets in macroeconomic finance. Unlike equities or bonds, it generates no cash flow — no dividend, no coupon. Its value is therefore largely driven by opportunity cost: what an investor gives up by holding gold instead of a yield-bearing asset.

The 10-year US Treasury yield — and more precisely its real component (nominal yield minus inflation expectations) — is the canonical measure of that opportunity cost. When real yields rise, the relative attractiveness of gold falls, and vice versa.

This relationship is well documented in the academic literature:

-   **Jermann (2023, NBER)**: a no-arbitrage pricing model calibrated on 10Y real US Treasury rates successfully replicates gold price fluctuations since 2007.
-   **Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago (2021)**: a 1 percentage point rise in the long-term real rate is associated with a 13.1% decline in the real gold price over the period 1971–2021.
-   **J.P. Morgan Private Bank (2026)**: documents a structural break post-2022, where the inverse correlation weakened — gold became asymmetrically reactive, rising when yields fall but resisting when yields rise.

This project investigates this relationship empirically using daily data from June 2011 to June 2026, sourced from the Alpha Vantage API.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Hypotheses

### H1 — Long-run equilibrium relationship

The 10Y US Treasury yield is a significant negative predictor of the gold price, and a stable long-run cointegrating relationship exists between the two series.

Formally, if both series are integrated of order 1 — i.e. I(1) — we expect to find at least one cointegrating vector such that:

$$\text{Gold}_t = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{Yield}_t + \varepsilon_t$$

where $\varepsilon_t$ is stationary, and $\beta < 0$.

### H2 — Mean-reverting residual

The residual $\varepsilon_t$ from the long-run relationship is mean-reverting. Deviations from equilibrium are temporary and self-correcting.

This implies that when gold is overpriced relative to what the yield level implies, it will tend to revert downward — and vice versa. The normalized residual therefore constitutes an analyticalsignal:

$$z_t = \frac{\varepsilon_t - \mu_\varepsilon}{\sigma_\varepsilon}$$

$$z_t > +2 \Rightarrow \text{gold expensive relative to yields}$$ $$z_t < -2 \Rightarrow \text{gold cheap relative to yields}$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Analytical Framework

The analysis proceeds in four steps:

1.  **Stationarity testing** — Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) tests on each series in level and first difference, to confirm both are I(1).

2.  **Cointegration testing** — Johansen test to determine whether a long-run equilibrium relationship exists between gold and the 10Y yield.

3.  **VECM estimation** — Vector Error Correction Model to estimate the long-run cointegrating vector and the speed of adjustment of each variable toward equilibrium.

4.  **Rolling OLS** — Estimation of $\beta$ on a rolling 2-year window to assess the stability of the relationship over time, and in particular to capture the structural break observed post-2022.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Data

| Series                    | Source        | Endpoint              | Frequency |
|---------------------------|---------------|-----------------------|-----------|
| Gold price (USD/oz)       | Alpha Vantage | `GOLD_SILVER_HISTORY` | Daily     |
| 10Y US Treasury Yield (%) | Alpha Vantage | `TREASURY_YIELD`      | Daily     |

Sample period: **June 1, 2011 — June 1, 2026** — 3,704 observations.
